title: Data Literacy: Spreadsheets, Charts and Business Metrics
subtitle: Use a free phone spreadsheet to collect, clean, analyse and present real data, and make decisions based on evidence instead of guesswork.
description: A practical course for women running businesses, groups and programmes in Nigeria and across Africa. You will learn the core vocabulary of data, build tidy spreadsheets in Google Sheets, summarise and chart results honestly, track profit and customer metrics, and present findings that clients, employers, donors and communities act on.
outcomes: Turn a business or community question into data you can collect and analyse
Build a tidy Google Sheets log and use SUM, AVERAGE, MEDIAN, SUMIF and COUNTIF
Clean messy records by removing duplicates, fixing spellings and checking extreme values
Choose and read charts correctly and spot misleading numbers and graphs
Calculate gross margin, net profit, average order value, repeat rate and break-even
Present findings in a one-page report and a short WhatsApp summary that lead to action
audience: Women entrepreneurs, group treasurers, programme staff and job seekers who can use a smartphone and want to work confidently with numbers.
tools: A smartphone (Android or iPhone) or a computer
A free Google account and the Google Sheets app
A calculator (the phone calculator is fine)
Your own records: a sales notebook, receipts, bank or wallet history, or group registers
Some mobile data or Wi-Fi for setup and syncing

modules.title: Data foundations: questions, numbers and safe tools
modules.overview: You will learn what data is, the handful of words and calculations that unlock almost every report, and how to set up a free spreadsheet on your phone safely. By the end of the module you can turn a question about your business or group into data you can actually collect.

lessons.title: What data is and how it answers everyday questions
objectives: Define data and give examples from your own work or community
Tell the difference between numbers, categories, dates and free text
Turn a vague worry into a clear question that data can answer
Follow the five-step path from question to decision

blocks.text: **Data** is simply recorded facts. The number of bottles of zobo you sold on Saturday is data. So is the name of the customer who paid by transfer, the date a cooperative member made her contribution, and the comment a client left on your WhatsApp status. When facts are written down in an organised way, you can count them, compare them and learn from them. When they stay in your head, they turn into guesses.

**Data literacy** is the ability to read, work with, question and talk about data. It does not mean advanced mathematics. It means you can look at a sales record, a chart in a newspaper or a donor report and ask: what does this really show, is it accurate, and what should I do about it?

blocks.name: data-at-work
blocks.alt: A woman working with charts and data on a screen
blocks.caption: Data literacy starts with recording everyday facts and asking good questions of them.

blocks.text: Four kinds of data you will meet

head: Kind
What it looks like
Example
What you can do with it
rows: Amounts you can add or average
Sum, average, compare, find highest and lowest
Count how many fall in each group, find the most common
Group by day, week or month, see trends
Read for themes, count repeated complaints

blocks.text: Numbers come in two kinds. **Counts** are whole numbers, such as 3 customers or 12 tubers of yam. **Measurements** can have parts, such as 1.5 litres or 2.75 kg. Categories are not numbers even when they look like them: a member ID like 0457 is a label, so it makes no sense to add member IDs together.
Where your data comes from

items: **Records you already keep:** a sales notebook, receipts, a cooperative contribution register, attendance lists.
**Digital traces:** your bank or Opay and Moniepoint transaction history, POS slips, WhatsApp Business catalogue views, Paystack payment reports.
**Data you collect on purpose:** a short survey on Google Forms, a tally sheet at a market stall, a phone call to past customers.
**Data other people publish:** for example, the National Bureau of Statistics publishes inflation and price reports you can read online.

blocks.text: The first three are **primary data**: you collected it yourself for your own purpose. The last is **secondary data**: someone else collected it. Secondary data can save time, but you must check who made it, when and how.
Start with a question, not a spreadsheet

Many people start by collecting everything and end up with a notebook full of numbers they never use. Good analysts start with a clear question. A vague worry such as "business is slow" becomes useful when you sharpen it: "Which days of the week bring the most sales?" or "Did more customers pay by transfer in September than in August?" A good question names what you will measure and over what period.

blocks.title: From question to decision
items: Ask a clear question
Collect the right data
Organise it in a table
Analyse and compare
Decide and act
blocks.caption: Every data task in this course follows these five steps, and the decision at the end often raises the next question.

blocks.title: Worked example: which day should she make extra zobo?
blocks.context: For example, Amaka sells chilled zobo near a bus park in Ibadan. She feels Saturdays are busy but often throws away unsold bottles on other days. She records sales for one week.
steps: Her question: "How many bottles do I sell on each day of the week?"
She writes a tally each evening: Mon 18, Tue 15, Wed 17, Thu 16, Fri 26, Sat 34, Sun 12.
She adds them: 18 + 15 + 17 + 16 + 26 + 34 + 12 = 138 bottles for the week.
She finds the average per day: 138 ÷ 7 = about 19.7 bottles.
She compares: Friday (26) and Saturday (34) are well above average; Sunday (12) is well below.
blocks.result: Amaka decides to make about 20 bottles on weekdays, about 30 on Friday, 35 on Saturday and only 12 on Sunday, and to keep recording for three more weeks to check the pattern holds.

blocks.title: One week is a start, not a proof
blocks.text: A single week can be unusual because of rain, a public holiday or a church event. Collect at least three or four weeks before making a big change, such as buying more stock on credit.
Data, information and insight

It helps to separate three ideas. **Data** is the raw record: 34 bottles on Saturday. **Information** is data organised so it means something: Saturday sells almost three times as much as Sunday. **Insight** is what you understand and act on: make more on Saturday, less on Sunday, and stop wasting stock. Your aim in every task is to move from data to insight.

Notice what happened in the example. Amaka did not need any app. She needed a clear question, honest daily records and simple arithmetic. In the rest of this course you will do the same steps faster and more accurately in a spreadsheet, and you will learn to present the result so others trust it.

takeaways: Data is recorded facts; writing them down turns guesses into evidence.
Numbers can be added and averaged; categories can only be counted.
Start with a sharp question that names what you measure and when.
Question, collect, organise, analyse, decide: the same five steps every time.

activity.title: Turn a worry into a data question
steps: Write down one thing about your business, job or group that you are unsure about.
Rewrite it as a clear question that names what you will measure and for how long.
List the data you need and say whether each item is a number, category, date or text.
Decide where the data will come from (notebook, bank history, survey) and start recording today.
activity.evidence: A photo or note showing your original worry, your sharpened question and your list of data types.

lessons.title: The vocabulary of data: rows, columns, averages and percentages
objectives: Name the parts of a data table: record, variable, value and cell
Calculate the mean, median, mode and range of a small set of numbers
Choose between mean and median when one value is very large or small
Calculate a percentage and a percentage change correctly

blocks.text: Data people use a few words again and again. Once you know them, spreadsheets, reports and charts become much easier to read. This lesson covers the words for the parts of a table and the five calculations you will use most.
The parts of a data table

items: **Dataset:** the whole collection of records about one topic, for example all sales in September.
**Record (row):** one item or event, such as one sale or one member. Each row is one record.
**Variable (column):** one thing you measure about every record, such as date, item, quantity or amount.
**Value:** a single entry, such as "Rice" or 2,500.
**Cell:** the box where a row and column meet. In a spreadsheet, cell B4 is column B, row 4.

blocks.name: data-table
blocks.alt: A table of data with rows and columns
blocks.caption: Each row is one record and each column is one variable; keeping this rule makes every calculation easier.

blocks.text: Spreadsheets also care about **data types**. A cell can hold a number, text, a date or a formula. If you type "2k" instead of 2000, the spreadsheet sees text and will leave it out of totals. Typing amounts as plain numbers, without the naira sign or words, keeps every calculation correct. You can add the ₦ sign later with formatting.
Five calculations that answer most questions

head: Measure
What it tells you
How to find it
rows: The typical value if everything were shared equally
Add all values, divide by how many there are
Sort from smallest to largest, take the middle one (or the mean of the two middle ones)
The value that appears most often
How spread out the values are

blocks.title: Worked example: what does a typical customer spend?
blocks.context: For example, Halima runs a small provisions kiosk in Kaduna. On Tuesday morning she records what seven customers spent, in naira: 1,500; 2,000; 2,000; 2,500; 3,000; 3,500; 20,000. The 20,000 was a caterer buying in bulk.
steps: Median: the values are already sorted. The middle (4th) value is ₦2,500.
Mode: ₦2,000 appears twice, more than any other value.
Compare: only one of the seven customers spent more than ₦4,929, so the mean does not describe a typical customer.
blocks.result: The median of ₦2,500 is the better answer to "what does a typical customer spend?" because one bulk buyer pulled the mean far upwards.

blocks.title: Mean or median?
items: Use the mean
Use the median
right: One or two values are extreme
blocks.caption: An extreme value moves the mean a lot but barely moves the median.

blocks.text: Percentages and percentage change

A **percentage** compares a part with a whole. If 18 of your 60 customers paid by POS, that is 18 ÷ 60 × 100 = 30%. Percentages let you compare groups of different sizes fairly: 30 transfers out of 50 sales (60%) is a bigger share than 40 transfers out of 100 sales (40%), even though 40 is the larger number.

A **percentage change** tells you how much something grew or fell compared with where it started. The formula is: (new value minus old value) ÷ old value × 100. If sales were ₦250,000 in August and ₦300,000 in September, the change is (300,000 minus 250,000) ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 20% growth. Always divide by the **old** value, not the new one. Dividing by the new value here would give about 16.7%, which is wrong.

blocks.title: Percentage points are not percent
blocks.text: If the share of customers paying by transfer moves from 40% to 50%, it rose by 10 percentage points, but by 25% in relative terms (10 ÷ 40 × 100). Reports sometimes mix these up, so check which one is meant.

blocks.title: Worked example: comparing two weeks fairly
blocks.context: For example, Halima wants to know whether more of her customers are paying by transfer. In week 1 she had 50 sales and 30 were transfers. In week 2 she had 80 sales and 40 were transfers.
steps: Week 1 share: 30 ÷ 50 × 100 = 60% transfers.
Week 2 share: 40 ÷ 80 × 100 = 50% transfers.
Change in share: 50% minus 60% = a fall of 10 percentage points.
Change in number of transfers: (40 minus 30) ÷ 30 × 100 = about 33% more transfers.
blocks.result: Both statements are true: she received more transfers in week 2, but transfers made up a smaller share of her sales because cash sales grew faster. A careful report says both.

blocks.text: Rates and ratios

A **rate** is a count over a period or per group, for example 12 new members per month, or 3 complaints per 100 orders. A **ratio** compares two amounts, for example 2 cash payments for every 5 transfers, written 2:5. Rates per 100 or per 1,000 let you compare a small group with a big one.

takeaways: Each row is a record, each column a variable, each box a cell.
Mean adds and divides; median is the middle; mode is the most common.
When one value is extreme, report the median.
Percentage change = (new minus old) ÷ old × 100.

activity.title: Calculate the five measures on real numbers
steps: Write down 7 to 10 real amounts from your own records, such as daily sales or what customers spent.
Sort them from smallest to largest.
Calculate the mean, median, mode and range by hand or with a phone calculator.
Calculate one percentage (for example, the share paid by transfer) and one percentage change between two weeks.
Write one sentence saying whether the mean or the median better describes a typical day.
activity.evidence: A photo of your worked calculations with the one-sentence conclusion.

lessons.title: Setting up your phone tools and keeping data safe
objectives: Install and open Google Sheets and create your first named spreadsheet
Protect your account and files with a strong password, two-step verification and correct sharing
Apply the basic principles of the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 to records about other people
Recognise common scams that target business data and money

blocks.text: You can do almost everything in this course with a smartphone and a free Google account. **Google Sheets** is a free spreadsheet app made by Google. It runs on Android and iPhone and in any web browser, and it saves your work automatically to Google Drive, so a lost or broken phone does not mean lost records. Microsoft Excel works in a very similar way, so the skills carry over if your office uses Excel.
Getting set up

items: Install **Google Sheets** from the Play Store or App Store. It is often already installed on Android phones.
Sign in with your Gmail address. If you do not have one, create a Google account first.
Tap the **+** button and choose **New spreadsheet**.
Tap the file name at the top ("Untitled spreadsheet") and give it a clear name, such as "Shop sales 2026".
Type a heading in cell A1, such as Date, and a value in A2, then close the app and open it again to see that it saved.
Optional: in the Google Drive or Sheets settings, turn on **offline** access for important files so you can work without data and let them sync later.

blocks.name: spreadsheets
blocks.alt: A person working with spreadsheets on a screen
blocks.caption: A free spreadsheet app on your phone is the only tool you need for this course.

blocks.title: Saving data bundles
blocks.text: Spreadsheets with text and numbers are small files. Most data is used when you first install the app and when you open charts or many images. Do heavier work on Wi-Fi when you can, and keep files focused rather than adding photos inside them.
Protecting your account and files

items: Use a strong, unique password for your Google account: a long phrase is easier to remember and harder to guess than a short word with numbers.
Turn on **2-Step Verification** in your Google account security settings, so a stolen password alone cannot open your files.
When you share a file, choose the right level: **Viewer** can only look, **Commenter** can suggest, **Editor** can change everything. Give Editor only to people who truly need it.
Avoid "Anyone with the link" for files that contain names, phone numbers or money records.
Use **File, Version history** to see and restore earlier versions if someone deletes or changes data by mistake.

blocks.text: Data about other people is a responsibility

Customer phone numbers, member contributions and addresses are **personal data**. Nigeria has a law about this: the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023**, enforced by the **Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC)**. For a small business or community group, the practical lessons are simple: collect only what you need, tell people why you are collecting it, keep it secure, use it only for that purpose, and do not pass it to others without permission.

The Act also gives people rights over their own data, such as the right to know what you hold about them and to ask for it to be corrected. In practice, that means keeping records tidy enough that you can find one person's entries quickly, and correcting mistakes when a member or customer points them out. If you ever handle data for a larger organisation, ask whether it has a data protection policy and follow it.

blocks.title: Before you record personal data
items: Do I really need this?
Did I explain why?
Is the file protected?
Who can see it?
When will I delete it?
blocks.caption: Five quick checks that keep you on the right side of good data practice and the law.

blocks.title: Worked example: a safe contribution register
blocks.context: For example, Fatima is treasurer of a 25-member women's savings group in Kano. Members used to post payment screenshots in the WhatsApp group, where everyone could see everyone else's account details.
steps: She creates a Google Sheet called "Group contributions 2026" with columns: Member code, Date, Amount (₦), Payment method.
She uses codes (M01 to M25) instead of full names, and keeps the list matching codes to names in a separate file only she and the chairperson can open.
She shares the main sheet as **Viewer** with members so they can confirm their own entries, and as **Editor** only with the financial secretary.
She turns on 2-Step Verification and asks members to send payment proof to her privately, not in the group.
blocks.result: Members can check that their contributions are recorded, account details no longer appear in a group chat of 25 people, and if her phone is lost, the record is still safe in Google Drive.

blocks.title: Common scams aimed at your data
blocks.text: Never share a one-time password (OTP), your BVN or your banking PIN with anyone, even someone who says they are from your bank, a payment app or Google. Be careful with links that ask you to "verify" your account, and check payment alerts in your actual bank app, not only by SMS or a screenshot, before releasing goods.

takeaways: Google Sheets is free, works on phones and saves automatically.
Strong password plus 2-Step Verification protects your records.
Share as Viewer by default; give Editor only when needed.
Collect only the personal data you need and keep it secure, in line with the NDPA 2023.

activity.title: Set up a safe workbook
steps: Install Google Sheets, sign in and create a spreadsheet with a clear name.
Add column headings for the data you chose in Lesson 1.
Turn on 2-Step Verification on your Google account.
Share the file with one trusted person as Viewer and check what they can and cannot do.
Write two sentences on what personal data you will collect and why you need it.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your named spreadsheet with headings, and a screenshot of the sharing settings (hide any private emails).

quiz.q: Amaka records the payment method for each sale as cash, transfer or POS. What kind of data is this?
options: A measurement that can be averaged
A category that can be counted
quiz.explain: Payment method is a label from a short list, so it is categorical data. You can count how many sales fall in each category, but you cannot average it.

quiz.q: Seven customers spend ₦1,500, ₦2,000, ₦2,000, ₦2,500, ₦3,000, ₦3,500 and ₦20,000. Which figure best describes a typical customer?
quiz.explain: One bulk buyer pulls the mean far upwards. The median, the middle value, is not affected by that extreme and describes the typical customer better.

quiz.q: Sales were ₦250,000 in August and ₦300,000 in September. What is the percentage change?
quiz.explain: (300,000 minus 250,000) ÷ 250,000 × 100 = 20%. Always divide by the old value.

quiz.q: Which question is best suited to being answered with data?
options: How many bottles do I sell on each day of the week over the next four weeks?
Why is business so slow these days?
Will customers like me more next year?
quiz.explain: A good data question names what will be measured and over what period. The other options are vague and do not say what to record.

quiz.q: A savings group treasurer wants members to check their own entries without being able to change the record. Which sharing setting should she use for members?
options: Anyone with the link can edit
quiz.explain: Viewer lets members see the sheet but not change it. Editor access should go only to the people who maintain the record.

modules.title: Working with spreadsheets: tables, formulas and charts
modules.overview: This module takes you from a blank sheet to a clear monthly summary and a chart you can share. You will build a tidy sales log, use the formulas that do most of the work, and choose and read charts correctly.

lessons.title: Building a tidy data table with your first formulas
objectives: Lay out a data table using the tidy data rules
Write formulas with SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX and MIN
Use cell references and the fill handle to calculate a whole column
Freeze the header row and format amounts as naira

blocks.text: Most spreadsheet problems start with layout, not formulas. If the table is arranged well, every calculation in this course takes seconds. If it is messy, even simple totals go wrong. This lesson shows you the layout that analysts call **tidy data**, then the first five formulas you will use every week.
The tidy data rules

items: **One row per record.** Each sale, member payment or order gets its own row.
**One column per variable.** Date in one column, item in another, quantity in another. Do not write "3 bags rice" in one cell; split it into Quantity: 3 and Item: Rice.
**One header row at the top.** Short, clear headings in row 1, such as Date, Item, Qty, Unit price, Amount, Payment.
**No merged cells, no blank rows, no totals in the middle.** Keep totals in a separate area or a summary sheet.
**Consistent values.** Always write "Rice", not sometimes "rice" or "Rice (50kg)". Always enter dates the same way.

blocks.title: Notebook habit versus tidy table
items: Messy layout
Tidy layout
blocks.caption: The tidy layout is what lets formulas, sorting, filters and charts work without errors.

blocks.name: data-input
blocks.alt: A person entering data into a form on a screen
blocks.caption: Entering one record per row, the same way every time, is the habit that makes analysis easy.

blocks.text: Why does this matter so much? Because a spreadsheet only understands what is in each cell. If one cell says "3 bags rice", the spreadsheet cannot multiply it, count it as rice or add it to a total. Splitting facts into their own columns is a few extra taps when you enter data, and it saves hours later.
How formulas work

A **formula** always starts with an equals sign (=). It can use numbers, cell references and functions. A **cell reference** like D2 means "whatever is in cell D2". If the value in D2 changes, every formula that uses D2 updates by itself. A **range** like E2:E31 means all the cells from E2 down to E31. A **function** is a ready-made calculation, such as SUM or AVERAGE.

head: Formula
What it does
Example result
rows: Multiplies quantity by unit price for one row
Adds every amount in the range

blocks.text: Filling a formula down a column

You do not need to type the Amount formula in every row. Type =C2*D2 in cell E2. On a computer, drag the small square at the bottom right of the cell (the **fill handle**) down the column. On the phone app, tap the cell, choose Copy, select the cells below and Paste. The spreadsheet adjusts the references for each row automatically: row 3 becomes =C3*D3, row 4 becomes =C4*D4, and so on. This is called a **relative reference**.

blocks.title: Worked example: a one-week sales log
blocks.context: For example, Chioma sells foodstuff from a stall in Onitsha main market. She sets up a Google Sheet with the headings Date, Item, Qty, Unit price (₦), Amount (₦), Payment in row 1.
steps: Row 2: 02/09/2026, Rice (50kg bag), 1, 80000, =C2*D2 gives 80,000, Transfer.
Row 3: 02/09/2026, Beans (paint bucket), 4, 4500, =C3*D3 gives 18,000, Cash.
Row 4: 03/09/2026, Garri (paint bucket), 6, 2500, =C4*D4 gives 15,000, POS.
She copies the Amount formula down to row 40 and keeps adding a row for every sale during the week.
In a separate area she types: Total =SUM(E2:E40), Number of sales =COUNT(E2:E40), Average sale =AVERAGE(E2:E40), Biggest sale =MAX(E2:E40).
blocks.result: Every time she adds a sale, her total, count and averages update by themselves. She no longer adds up the notebook at night, and her totals are free of arithmetic slips. (Prices here are approximate examples; use your own.)

blocks.text: Small settings that save trouble

items: **Freeze the header row** (on a computer: View, Freeze, 1 row; on the phone: tap the row number, then Freeze) so the headings stay visible as you scroll down.
**Format amounts as currency or with thousand separators** using the Format options, instead of typing the ₦ sign yourself, so the cells stay numbers.
**Set the spreadsheet locale to Nigeria** (File, Settings on the browser version) so dates are read as day/month/year. Otherwise 03/09/2026 may be read as 9 March instead of 3 September.
**Keep raw data on one sheet** and do calculations on a second sheet. Tap the + at the bottom to add a sheet and name it "Summary".

blocks.title: If a total looks too small
blocks.text: A common reason is that some amounts were typed as text, for example with a space, a ₦ sign, a comma in the wrong place or "k". Text is often left-aligned while numbers are right-aligned. Retype those cells as plain numbers and the total will correct itself.

takeaways: Tidy data: one row per record, one column per variable, one header row.
Every formula starts with = and uses cell references so it updates itself.
SUM, AVERAGE, COUNT, MAX, MIN and MEDIAN answer most first questions.
Keep amounts as plain numbers and set the locale so dates read correctly.

lessons.title: Summarising a month of sales: SUMIF, COUNTIF and shares of the total
objectives: Total and count records by category using SUMIF and COUNTIF
Calculate each category's share of the total as a percentage
Sort and filter a table to answer a specific question
Turn a monthly summary into one or two clear business decisions

blocks.text: A month of sales might be 200 or 300 rows. Nobody can see a pattern by scrolling through that many lines. The skill in this lesson is **summarising**: turning many rows into a short table that answers a question, such as "Which items bring in the most money?" or "How do most customers pay?"
Two functions that summarise by category

**SUMIF** adds up only the rows that match a condition. Its pattern is =SUMIF(range to check, what to look for, range to add). For example, =SUMIF(B2:B300,"Rice",E2:E300) looks down column B for the word Rice and adds the matching amounts from column E.

**COUNTIF** counts the rows that match a condition. Its pattern is =COUNTIF(range to check, what to look for). For example, =COUNTIF(F2:F300,"Transfer") counts how many sales were paid by transfer. Instead of typing "Rice" inside the formula, you can point to a cell that contains the word, such as =SUMIF(B$2:B$300,H2,E$2:E$300). The $ signs lock the range so it does not move when you copy the formula down.

blocks.name: financial-data
blocks.alt: Financial charts and figures on a screen
blocks.caption: A short summary table turns hundreds of rows into a few numbers you can act on.

blocks.title: Worked example: where does the money come from?
blocks.context: For example, Ada runs a provisions shop in Abeokuta. Her September log has 220 sales worth ₦400,000 in total. She builds a summary sheet with each item in column H and SUMIF formulas next to them.
steps: SUMIF results by item: Rice ₦180,000; Beans ₦72,000; Palm oil ₦60,000; Garri ₦48,000; Others ₦40,000. Check: these add to ₦400,000, the same as =SUM of all amounts.
Share of total: Rice 180,000 ÷ 400,000 × 100 = 45%; Beans 18%; Palm oil 15%; Garri 12%; Others 10%. Check: the shares add to 100%.
COUNTIF by payment method: Transfer 120, Cash 70, POS 30. Check: 120 + 70 + 30 = 220 sales.
Payment shares: Transfer 120 ÷ 220 × 100 = about 54.5%; Cash about 31.8%; POS about 13.6%.
Average sale: ₦400,000 ÷ 220 = about ₦1,818.
blocks.result: Rice alone brings in almost half of her sales, so running out of rice is her biggest risk; she decides to keep a minimum of two bags in stock. More than half of payments are transfers, so she prints her account details clearly at the counter and checks every alert in her bank app before releasing goods.

blocks.title: From rows to a decision
items: Decision
Shares of the total
Totals by category
Hundreds of raw rows
blocks.caption: Each layer is smaller and more useful than the one beneath it; always check that totals at each layer agree.

blocks.text: Always check your summary adds up

A summary is only trustworthy if it agrees with the raw data. After any SUMIF table, add the category totals and compare them with =SUM of the whole amount column. If they differ, some rows have a category spelled differently ("rice" with a space, for instance) or left blank. Fixing those is the subject of Module 3, Lesson 1.

You can also count with two conditions at once using **COUNTIFS** and **SUMIFS**. For example, =SUMIFS(E2:E300,B2:B300,"Rice",F2:F300,"POS") adds only the rice sales paid by POS. Notice that in SUMIFS the range to add comes first, the opposite of SUMIF. When a formula gives a strange result, check the order of its parts first.
Sorting and filtering

items: **Sort** puts rows in order. Select the whole table first, not just one column, otherwise the amounts get separated from their items. Sorting by Amount from largest to smallest shows your biggest sales at the top.

**Filter** hides rows you do not need for now without deleting them. In the browser version, choose Data, Create a filter, then tap the filter icon on a heading, for example to show only POS payments or only one week.
**Filter views** (browser version) let you save a filter without changing what other people see in a shared sheet.

blocks.title: Pivot tables, when you are ready
blocks.text: A pivot table builds a summary like Ada's automatically. In the browser version of Google Sheets, select your table and choose Insert, Pivot table, then add Item as Rows and Amount as Values (SUM). Learn SUMIF first so you understand what the pivot table is doing.
Asking the next question

A good summary usually raises a new question. Ada might now ask: are rice sales steady through the month, or do they jump at month end when salaries are paid? To answer that, she could add a Week column and use SUMIF by week. In data work, one clear answer often leads straight to the next useful question, and that is a sign you are doing it right.

takeaways: SUMIF adds by category; COUNTIF counts by category.
Share of total = category ÷ grand total × 100, and shares should add to 100%.
Check that category totals match the overall SUM before trusting a summary.
Select the whole table before sorting so rows stay together.

activity.title: Summarise your own records
steps: Use the log you built in Lesson 1 or at least 30 rows of real records.
List each category (item, service or payment method) in a summary area.
Use SUMIF to total amounts and COUNTIF to count records for each category.
Calculate each category's percentage of the total and check that they add to 100%.
Write two decisions you would make based on the summary.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your summary table with percentages and your two written decisions.

lessons.title: Choosing, building and reading charts
objectives: Choose the right chart type for comparisons, trends and parts of a whole
Create a chart in Google Sheets and add a clear title and labels
Read a chart by checking its title, axes, units and scale
Get feedback on a chart and improve it

blocks.text: A good chart lets someone understand your numbers in a few seconds. A poor chart confuses them or, worse, misleads them. The secret is not fancy design: it is choosing the chart type that matches your question and labelling it honestly.
Match the chart to the question

head: Your question
Best chart
Why
rows: Lengths are easy to compare side by side
How did sales change week by week?
A line shows movement over time clearly
What share does each item have?
Pie chart, only with 2 to 5 slices
Shows parts of one whole; too many slices become unreadable
Is there a link between two measures?
Each dot is one record plotted on two measures
Charts show patterns; tables show precise numbers

blocks.name: charts
blocks.alt: A collection of bar, line and pie charts
blocks.caption: Different questions need different charts: bars to compare, lines for change over time, pies for a few parts of a whole.

blocks.text: Making a chart in Google Sheets

items: Select the cells you want to chart, including the heading row (for example, Week in column A and Sales in column B).
Tap **Insert** (the + on the phone) and choose **Chart**. Sheets suggests a chart type.
Change the type if needed: line for weeks or months, column or bar for categories.
Edit the chart title so it says what the chart shows and when, for example "Weekly sales, August to September 2026 (₦)".
Check the axis labels and units, then tap the tick to place the chart.
On a computer you can download the chart as an image (three dots on the chart, Download) to share on WhatsApp.

blocks.title: Worked example: is the business growing?
blocks.context: For example, Ruth sells small chops for events and walk-in customers in Port Harcourt. She enters six weeks of sales in naira: Week 1: 52,000; Week 2: 58,000; Week 3: 49,000; Week 4: 61,000; Week 5: 70,000; Week 6: 66,000.
steps: Because the question is about change over time, she chooses a line chart with weeks along the bottom.
She calculates the six-week total: ₦356,000, and the weekly mean: 356,000 ÷ 6 = about ₦59,333.
Week 4 to Week 5 change: (70,000 minus 61,000) ÷ 61,000 × 100 = about 14.8% growth.
Week 5 to Week 6 change: (66,000 minus 70,000) ÷ 70,000 × 100 = about 5.7% fall.
She notes that Week 3 was a week of heavy rain with fewer walk-in customers, and writes this as a note beside the chart.
blocks.result: The line moves up overall even with ups and downs: the last three weeks are all above the six-week average. Her chart title reads "Weekly sales trending up, Weeks 1 to 6 (₦)" with a short note explaining the Week 3 dip.

blocks.title: Five checks when reading any chart
items: What does the title claim?
What do the axes measure?
What are the units?
Does the scale start at zero?
Who made it, from what data?
blocks.caption: Run these checks on every chart you make or receive before you believe its message.

blocks.text: Common chart mistakes to avoid

items: **Too many slices in a pie.** Above about five slices, group the small ones into "Others" or switch to a bar chart.
**Unsorted bars.** Sort categories from largest to smallest so the reader sees the ranking at a glance.
**Missing units.** "Sales: 70" could mean 70 bottles, ₦70 or ₦70,000. Put units in the title or axis label.
**Mixing time periods.** Do not compare a full month with a half month on the same chart without saying so.
**Charting the wrong measure.** If customer numbers changed a lot, the share of sales may tell a fairer story than raw totals.

blocks.text: Reading a chart carefully

When someone sends you a chart, read it from the outside in. First the **title**: what is it claiming? Then the **axes**: what is measured along the bottom and up the side? Then the **units**: naira, thousands of naira, percent? Then the **scale**: on a bar chart, the value axis should start at zero, otherwise small differences look huge. Finally, the **source**: who collected the data, how many records, and over what period?
The feedback loop

Before you share a chart widely, show it to one person who did not make it and ask: "What is the main message?" If they cannot say it in one sentence, improve the chart: shorten the title into a message, remove extra colours, sort bars from largest to smallest, or remove a chart element that distracts. Then ask again. Two quick rounds usually turn an average chart into a clear one.

blocks.title: Fewer colours, clearer message
blocks.text: Use one colour for all bars and a second, stronger colour only for the bar you want people to notice. Avoid 3D effects; they make values harder to compare.

takeaways: Bar for comparing categories, line for change over time, pie only for a few parts.
A chart title should state what it shows, the period and the units.
On bar charts the value axis should start at zero.
Test every chart on one person: can they state the message in one sentence?

activity.title: Make a chart and test it
steps: Choose one question from your own data that is about a comparison or a trend.
Build the matching chart in Google Sheets with a clear title, units and labelled axes.
Show it to one person and ask them to state the main message in one sentence.
Improve the chart based on their answer and save both versions.
activity.evidence: Screenshots of the first and improved charts, plus one line describing the feedback you received.

quiz.q: Chioma wants the total of all amounts in cells E2 to E40. Which formula is correct?
quiz.explain: Formulas start with =, and a range is written with a colon. =E2+E40 would only add two cells.

quiz.q: Ada's SUMIF totals by item add up to ₦385,000, but =SUM of the whole Amount column is ₦400,000. What is the most likely cause?
options: Some rows have the item spelled differently or left blank
quiz.explain: When category totals fall short of the grand total, some rows did not match any category, usually because of spelling differences, extra spaces or blanks.

quiz.q: Ruth wants to show how her sales changed over six weeks. Which chart should she use?
quiz.explain: A line chart shows change over time most clearly, with weeks along the bottom.

quiz.q: Out of 220 sales, 120 were paid by transfer. What share of sales is that?
Chioma sorts only the Amount column from largest to smallest without selecting the rest of the table. What is the risk?
options: Amounts become separated from their items and dates
quiz.explain: Sorting a single column breaks the link between each amount and the rest of its row. Always select the whole table before sorting.

quiz.q: A bar chart in a flyer shows one bar three times taller than another, but the values are 95 and 100. What should you check first?
options: Whether the value axis starts at zero
Whether it is a pie chart
quiz.explain: If the axis starts at, say, 90 instead of zero, a small 5-point difference looks huge. Always check the scale.

modules.title: Trustworthy data: cleaning, honest analysis and business metrics
modules.overview: Numbers are only useful if they are accurate and honestly interpreted. In this module you will clean messy data, learn to spot bias, privacy risks and misleading claims, and track the handful of business metrics that show whether you are really making money.

lessons.title: Cleaning messy data: duplicates, spellings, blanks and typos
objectives: Identify the six most common data quality problems
Use TRIM, PROPER, Remove duplicates and COUNTIF to fix them
Prevent errors with dropdown lists using data validation
Keep a short cleaning log so others can trust your figures

blocks.text: Real data is rarely clean. People type quickly, two people record the same sale, a phone autocorrects a word, a zero gets added by mistake. Analysts often say that cleaning takes more time than analysis, and it is worth it: one wrong row can change a total, a ranking or a decision. This lesson gives you a routine to find and fix the usual problems.
Six common problems

head: Problem
What it looks like
Why it matters
rows: One group is split into three in summaries
"Rice " with a space at the end
SUMIF does not match it to "Rice"
An empty Amount or Branch cell
Records are missed or counted wrongly
Left out of SUM and AVERAGE

blocks.name: clean-up
blocks.alt: A person tidying and cleaning up items
blocks.caption: Cleaning removes the small errors that quietly distort totals and rankings.

blocks.text: Tools for each problem

items: **Extra spaces:** in a new column, type =TRIM(B2) and copy it down. TRIM removes spaces at the start and end and turns double spaces into single ones. In the browser version, Data, Data cleanup, Trim whitespace does the same in place.
**Inconsistent capital letters:** =PROPER(B2) turns "jos north" into "Jos North". You can combine them: =PROPER(TRIM(B2)).

**Duplicates:** in the browser version, select the table and choose Data, Data cleanup, Remove duplicates. To check before deleting, add a helper column with =COUNTIF(A$2:A$200,A2)>1, which shows TRUE for any value that appears more than once.
**Blanks:** =COUNTBLANK(E2:E200) tells you how many empty cells there are; use a filter to show only blanks and fill them from your notebook or receipts.
**Text numbers:** retype them as plain numbers, or use =VALUE(E2) for numbers stored as text.
**Typos and extremes:** use =MAX and =MIN on each numeric column. If the largest contribution is ₦500,000 in a group where most pay ₦5,000, check that row against the original record.

blocks.text: After cleaning a column with a formula, copy the clean column and use **Paste special, Values only** to replace the original. Otherwise the clean column still depends on the messy one, and deleting the messy one breaks it.

blocks.title: Worked example: cleaning a cooperative contribution list
blocks.context: For example, Grace is the new financial secretary of a cooperative in Jos with three branches. She receives a 60-row contribution list for September compiled from three branch WhatsApp reports. The SUM of the Amount column is ₦612,000.
steps: She applies =PROPER(TRIM()) to the Branch column. Five different spellings collapse into the three correct branch names.
A COUNTIF helper column on Receipt number flags 3 rows as TRUE. Each is a ₦5,000 payment posted by two branch secretaries. She deletes the extra copies: 3 × 5,000 = ₦15,000 removed.
=COUNTBLANK shows 2 empty Amount cells. She checks the receipts: both members paid ₦5,000, so she fills them in. The total rises by ₦10,000.
=MAX shows one entry of ₦50,000. The receipt says ₦5,000; she corrects it, reducing the total by ₦45,000.
New total: 612,000 minus 15,000 plus 10,000 minus 45,000 = ₦562,000, and it now matches the bank statement.
blocks.result: The cleaned list has 57 rows, three correct branch names and a total that agrees with the bank. Grace records each change in a short cleaning log so the executive can see exactly what was corrected and why.

blocks.title: The data cleaning cycle
items: Check totals and counts
Find the problems
Fix and log changes
Prevent repeat errors
Recheck against source
blocks.caption: Cleaning is a routine you repeat each month, not a one-time task.

blocks.text: Prevent errors at the point of entry

The best clean-up is the one you never need. **Data validation** lets you restrict what can be typed in a column. In Google Sheets, select the column, choose Data, Data validation, Add rule, and pick **Dropdown**. Enter the allowed values, such as Cash, Transfer, POS. Now anyone entering data picks from the list instead of typing, so spelling stays consistent. You can also set a rule that only accepts numbers between, say, 1,000 and 100,000 for a contribution column.

items: Use dropdowns for every category column: item, branch, payment method, status.
Use one shared form, such as Google Forms linked to a sheet, instead of collecting reports in different formats.
Highlight suspicious values automatically with Format, Conditional formatting, for example amounts above a limit in red.
Keep the original raw file untouched and clean a copy, so you can always go back.

blocks.title: Keep a cleaning log
blocks.text: A simple second sheet with four columns, Date, Row or record, What was wrong, What you changed, makes your work checkable. Treasurers, auditors and donors trust figures more when they can see how they were corrected.

takeaways: Check totals, counts, blanks and the largest and smallest values first.
TRIM and PROPER fix spacing and capitals; COUNTIF finds duplicates.
Paste cleaned results as values and keep the raw file untouched.
Dropdown lists stop most spelling errors before they start.

activity.title: Clean a real list
steps: Take a real list of at least 30 rows (sales, members, attendance) and make a copy of it.
Record the starting row count and total.
Fix spaces and capitals with TRIM and PROPER, find duplicates with COUNTIF and count blanks with COUNTBLANK.
Check the MAX and MIN of each numeric column against your source records.
Add a dropdown to at least one category column and write a cleaning log.
activity.evidence: Before-and-after screenshots showing row counts and totals, plus your cleaning log sheet.

lessons.title: Honest analysis: privacy, bias and misleading claims
objectives: Anonymise personal data before sharing it
Spot sampling bias and low response rates in surveys
Explain why correlation does not prove causation
Recognise misleading charts and numbers, and avoid making them

blocks.text: Data can be accurate and still be used badly. It can expose people's private details, leave out the people who most need to be counted, or be presented in a way that pushes the reader to a wrong conclusion. Ethical data work protects people and tells the truth, even when the truth is less exciting.
Protect people first

items: **Collect the minimum.** If you only need to know how many women attended, you do not need their home addresses.
**Anonymise before sharing.** Replace names with codes (P01, P02) and remove phone numbers when sending a report to a donor, a WhatsApp group or a partner.
**Watch small groups.** If only one widow in a village group received support, reporting "1 widow in Ward 3" may identify her. Combine small groups or report them more broadly.
**Ask for consent.** On a survey, state at the top what the answers are for and who will see them, and make sensitive questions optional.

blocks.name: personal-data
blocks.alt: A personal profile card with protected details
blocks.caption: Before any report leaves your phone, check that no one can be identified who did not agree to it.

blocks.text: Screenshots are a frequent leak. A screenshot of a member list or payment record posted in a large WhatsApp group can be forwarded anywhere within minutes. Share a summary instead, or a version with codes in place of names.
Who is missing from the data?

**Bias** in data means the data leans one way and does not fairly represent the group you care about. A common cause is **sampling bias**: the people who answered are not like the people who did not. A survey shared only by WhatsApp link misses members without smartphones or data. A survey at a Saturday market misses women who work on Saturdays. Always ask: who was able to respond, and who was not?

Also look at the **response rate**: responses ÷ people asked × 100. A low response rate does not make results useless, but it means you should describe them as "of those who replied" rather than "members say".

blocks.title: Worked example: a survey that needs care
blocks.context: For example, the coordinator of a women's group in Enugu with 120 members sends a Google Forms link on WhatsApp asking which day members prefer for training. She receives 48 responses, and 36 choose Saturday.
steps: Response rate: 48 ÷ 120 × 100 = 40%.
Among respondents: 36 ÷ 48 × 100 = 75% prefer Saturday.
She notices that almost no older members responded; many of them use basic phones without data.
She asks branch leaders to collect answers from non-respondents by phone call or at the next meeting, using the same question.
She reports: "75% of the 48 members who replied online prefer Saturday; we are collecting answers from the other members before deciding."
blocks.result: Instead of claiming "75% of members want Saturday", she gives an honest picture and fills the gap, so the final decision reflects the whole group, not only those with smartphones.

blocks.title: Correlation versus causation
items: Correlation
Causation
right: One thing makes the other happen
blocks.caption: Two numbers rising together is a clue to investigate, not proof that one causes the other.

blocks.text: Correlation is not causation

If zobo sales and electric fan sales both rise from February to April, they are **correlated**: they move together. Zobo does not cause fan sales. Both are driven by a third factor, hot weather. When you see two measures move together, ask whether something else could explain both before concluding one causes the other. The fairest way to test a cause in a small business is to change one thing at a time, for example to run a price discount for two weeks while keeping everything else the same, and compare with similar weeks.
Misleading numbers and charts

items: **Cut-off axes** that make a small change look dramatic.
**Cherry-picked periods**, such as showing only the three best months.
**Big percentages from tiny numbers**: "sales up 100%" may mean from 2 to 4 orders.
**Averages that hide spread**: an average profit of ₦50,000 a month across members may hide that most earn far less.

**Investment schemes that show steady high returns.** Promises of fixed, high monthly returns, with charts and screenshots as "proof", are a classic warning sign of Ponzi schemes. Check any investment platform's registration with the Securities and Exchange Commission Nigeria before paying.

blocks.text: Your own honesty checklist

Before you send a report, read each claim and ask three questions. How many records or people is this based on? Over what period? What would someone who disagrees point out? If a finding only holds for one good week, say so. If a chart starts its axis above zero, either fix it or label it clearly. Reporting a disappointing result honestly builds more trust with a donor, an employer or your group than a polished but misleading one, and it helps you make better decisions yourself.

takeaways: Collect the minimum, anonymise before sharing and ask for consent.
Always ask who could not respond; report the response rate.
Correlation is a clue; causation needs a fair test.
Be suspicious of cut-off axes, cherry-picked periods and percentages from tiny numbers.

activity.title: Make a report safe and honest
steps: Take a list or summary that includes people's details and make an anonymised copy using codes.
Write down who might be missing from your data and how you could reach them.
Find one chart or claim in an advert, news story or WhatsApp message and apply the misleading-chart checks.
Rewrite one of your own findings as an honest sentence that includes how many people or records it is based on.
activity.evidence: The anonymised copy (screenshot), your note on missing groups, and the rewritten honest sentence.

lessons.title: Business metrics that matter: profit, margin, order value and repeat customers
objectives: Calculate revenue, gross profit, gross margin and net profit
Calculate average order value and repeat customer rate
Work out a simple break-even point
Set up a weekly dashboard with targets for three to five key metrics

blocks.text: A **metric** is a number you track to see how something is going. A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is one of the few metrics that matter most for your goal. Many small businesses track only sales, but high sales can still mean losing money. This lesson covers the metrics that tell you whether you are actually making money and keeping customers.
The core money metrics

head: Metric
Formula
What it tells you
rows: What you paid for the items you sold
The direct cost of those sales
Revenue minus cost of goods sold
Money left to cover other costs
How much of each ₦100 of sales is gross profit
Gross profit minus running costs (transport, data, rent, levies)
How much a typical sale brings in
Customers who bought more than once ÷ all customers × 100

blocks.name: metrics
blocks.caption: A few well-chosen metrics tell you more than a long list of numbers.

blocks.title: Worked example: September results for a provisions shop
blocks.context: For example, Ada (from Module 2) wants to know if her September sales of ₦400,000 were profitable. She checks her purchase receipts and expenses. All figures are illustrative.
steps: Revenue: ₦400,000 from 220 sales.
Cost of goods sold: ₦290,000. Gross profit: 400,000 minus 290,000 = ₦110,000.
Running costs: ₦20,000 for transport, phone data and her share of shop rent. Net profit: 110,000 minus 20,000 = ₦90,000, a net margin of 22.5%.
Average order value: 400,000 ÷ 220 = about ₦1,818.
Customers: she can identify 64 regular customers from transfer names and her notebook; 40 bought more than once. Repeat rate: 40 ÷ 64 × 100 = 62.5%.
blocks.result: Ada now knows that of every ₦100 she sells, about ₦27.50 is gross profit and about ₦22.50 is left after running costs. If her supplier raises prices and she does not adjust her selling prices, she will see it first in a falling gross margin.

blocks.text: Break-even: how much must you sell?

Your **break-even point** is the level of sales where you cover all your costs and make neither profit nor loss. For a single product the formula is: fixed costs ÷ (selling price minus cost per unit). The amount left from each sale after paying for the item itself is called the **contribution**.

For example, suppose a trader's fixed costs are ₦20,000 a month (stall fee, data, transport) and she sells a paint bucket of garri for ₦2,500 that cost her ₦2,000. Each bucket contributes ₦500. Break-even = 20,000 ÷ 500 = 40 buckets a month. Every bucket after the 40th adds ₦500 profit. If her supplier raises the cost to ₦2,200, the contribution falls to ₦300 and she needs about 67 buckets to break even, which shows why tracking costs matters as much as tracking sales.

blocks.title: From goal to raw data
items: Your goal
3 to 5 KPIs
Monthly and weekly measures
Daily records
blocks.caption: Choose KPIs from your goal downwards, then make sure your daily records capture what the KPIs need.

blocks.text: Build a simple weekly dashboard

items: Choose 3 to 5 KPIs linked to your goal, for example weekly revenue, gross margin, number of sales, repeat customers and stock-outs.
Create a sheet called Dashboard with one row per week and one column per KPI.
Use formulas that pull from your log, such as =SUMIFS(Amount, Week, 36) for revenue in week 36.
Add a Target row and use conditional formatting to colour cells green when on target and red when below.
Add one line chart for your most important KPI and review the dashboard every week at the same time.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading a dashboard week
blocks.context: For example, Ada sets weekly targets: revenue ₦100,000, gross margin at least 25%, and no more than one stock-out. In week 38 her dashboard shows revenue ₦104,000, gross margin 21% and zero stock-outs.
steps: Revenue is above target: 104,000 is 4% above 100,000, so the cell turns green.
Gross margin is red: 21% is below the 25% target, so each sale earned less than usual.
She filters the week's purchases and finds the price of a bag of rice from her supplier went up, while she kept her selling price the same.
She raises her rice price slightly and also asks a second supplier for a quote.
blocks.result: Without the margin KPI, Ada would have celebrated a good sales week while quietly earning less. The dashboard turned a hidden problem into a clear action.

blocks.title: Separate business and personal money
blocks.text: Metrics only work if business money is recorded separately. Use a separate account or wallet for the business where possible, and record any money you take for personal use as a withdrawal, not as a cost of goods.

takeaways: High sales do not guarantee profit: track gross margin and net profit.
Gross margin % = gross profit ÷ revenue × 100.
Break-even units = fixed costs ÷ (price minus cost per unit).
Pick 3 to 5 KPIs from your goal and review them weekly against targets.

activity.title: Calculate your own core metrics
steps: Gather one month of sales, purchase and expense records.
Calculate revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, gross margin and net profit.
Calculate average order value and, if you can identify customers, the repeat customer rate.
Work out the break-even point for your main product.
Set up a dashboard sheet with three KPIs and a target for each.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of your metrics calculations and dashboard with targets.

quiz.q: A contribution list shows Branch values "Jos North", "jos north" and "Jos  North". Which formula best standardises them?
quiz.explain: TRIM removes extra spaces and PROPER fixes capital letters, so all three versions become "Jos North".

quiz.q: Grace finds that =MAX of the Amount column is ₦50,000 in a group where most members pay ₦5,000. What should she do next?
options: Leave it, the maximum is always correct
Check that row against the original receipt
quiz.explain: Extreme values may be typing errors or genuine. Check the original record before changing or deleting anything.

quiz.q: A WhatsApp survey of 120 members gets 48 replies and 36 choose Saturday. Which report is most honest?
options: 75% of the 48 members who replied prefer Saturday
quiz.explain: Only 40% replied, and some groups may be missing, so the result should be described as applying to those who replied.

quiz.q: Revenue is ₦400,000 and cost of goods sold is ₦290,000. What is the gross margin?
Fixed costs are ₦20,000 a month. A product sells for ₦2,500 and costs ₦2,000. How many must be sold to break even?
quiz.explain: Each sale contributes ₦500. 20,000 ÷ 500 = 40 units.

quiz.q: Zobo sales and fan sales both rise from February to April. What is the best conclusion?
options: Zobo causes people to buy fans
Fans cause people to buy zobo
Both are probably driven by a third factor such as hot weather
quiz.explain: Correlation does not prove causation. Hot weather is a likely common cause of both.

modules.title: From analysis to impact: your workbook, your report, your plan
modules.overview: You will bring everything together into a data cleaning and insight workbook built on your own records, learn to present findings so clients, employers, donors or your community act on them, and finish with a certification checklist and a 90-day plan.

lessons.title: Building your data cleaning and insight workbook
objectives: Structure a workbook with raw, clean, summary, chart and notes sheets
Write a data dictionary that explains every column
Move from a question to a finding and a recommendation using your own data
Check your workbook for accuracy before submitting it

blocks.text: Your capstone is a **data cleaning and insight workbook**: one Google Sheets file that takes a real set of records from messy to meaningful. It proves you can do what this course teaches: ask a clear question, collect and clean data, summarise it, chart it honestly and draw a useful conclusion. Choose data you care about, such as your own sales, your group's contributions, attendance at your programme or orders for your service.
The five sheets

head: Sheet name
What goes in it
Course skill
rows: The original records exactly as collected, never edited
A cleaned copy with consistent labels, no duplicates or blanks
SUMIF and COUNTIF tables, shares, averages, medians and metrics
Two or three charts, each with a message title
Question, data dictionary, cleaning log, findings and recommendation

blocks.name: organizing-data
blocks.alt: A person arranging data into organised sections
blocks.caption: Separate sheets for raw, clean, summary, charts and notes make your work easy to follow and check.

blocks.text: Write a data dictionary

A **data dictionary** is a short table that explains each column: its name, what it means, its type and allowed values. It lets someone else understand and check your work without asking you. It also forces you to notice problems, such as a column where some amounts include delivery and some do not.

head: Column
Meaning
Type
Allowed values
rows: Day the order was paid for
Dress, Skirt and blouse, Kaftan, Other
Days from order date to delivery

blocks.title: Worked example: a tailor's three-month workbook
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi runs a tailoring business in Nyanya, Abuja. Her question: "Is my business growing, and why are some customers unhappy?" She enters 84 orders from July to September 2026 from her order book and WhatsApp chats.
steps: Raw and Clean: she standardises garment names, removes 2 duplicate orders she had entered twice, and fills missing delivery dates from her chats, leaving 84 valid orders.
Summary by month with COUNTIF and SUMIF: July 24 orders, ₦210,000; August 28 orders, ₦260,000; September 32 orders, ₦315,000. Total 84 orders, ₦785,000.
Growth: July to August (260,000 minus 210,000) ÷ 210,000 × 100 = about 23.8%; August to September about 21.2%.
Average order value: 785,000 ÷ 84 = about ₦9,345. Median days to deliver: 6.
On time: COUNTIF shows 10 late orders out of 84, about 11.9%. Filtering the late orders shows 8 of the 10 were group (aso ebi) orders of five or more outfits.
blocks.result: Finding: revenue grew every month, but group orders cause most late deliveries. Recommendation: quote group orders a longer delivery time and take a deposit earlier, then track whether the late rate falls below 5% next quarter.

blocks.title: A four-week workbook plan
items: Week 1: question and collection
Week 2: cleaning and dictionary
Week 3: summaries and charts
Week 4: findings and feedback
blocks.caption: About one focused hour, two or three times a week, is enough to finish the workbook in a month.

blocks.text: From numbers to a finding

A **finding** is a short statement of what the data shows, with a number: "Revenue grew about 21% from August to September." A **recommendation** says what to do because of it, and how you will know if it worked. Write no more than three findings. Each should answer part of your original question. If a summary is interesting but does not help answer your question, leave it out of the findings.

Good findings also say what the data cannot show. Ngozi's workbook shows that group orders were late more often, but not whether customers left because of it. She notes this as a limit and plans to ask her next ten group customers about their experience. Naming limits like this is part of honest analysis, and reviewers look for it.
Accuracy checks before you submit

items: The cleaned row count and total are explained in your cleaning log.
Category totals in the Summary sheet add up to the overall total.
Percentages of a whole add up to 100% (allow a small rounding difference).
Every chart has a message title, units and an axis that starts at zero where needed.
No personal names or phone numbers appear unless you have permission; codes are used instead.
Someone else can understand each column from the data dictionary.

blocks.title: If you have little data
blocks.text: You can start recording today and use four weeks of records. If that is not possible, use a dataset from your workplace or group with permission, removing personal details. Do not invent records: the point is to practise on real, imperfect data.

takeaways: Five sheets: Raw, Clean, Summary, Charts, Notes.
A data dictionary explains every column so others can check your work.
Write up to three findings with numbers, each answering your question.
Run the accuracy checks before you submit.

activity.title: Start your capstone workbook
steps: Create a new spreadsheet with the five named sheets.
Write your question at the top of the Notes sheet.

lessons.title: Presenting data so people act: reports, summaries and pitches
objectives: Adapt the same findings for a client, employer, donor or community audience
Structure a one-page report that leads with the answer
Write a clear WhatsApp-length data summary
Explain the difference between outputs and outcomes in impact reporting

blocks.text: Analysis only creates value when someone understands it and acts. A busy manager, a donor or a cooperative meeting will not read your spreadsheet. They need the answer, the key evidence and what you want them to do, in that order. This lesson shows you how to present data for different audiences.
Know your audience

head: Audience
What they care about
What to show
rows: Problems solved, time and money saved
The decision your analysis supports and its effect
Reach, outcomes, honest use of funds
Outputs, outcomes, costs per person, lessons learned
Fairness, transparency, what changes for them
Totals, who benefited, what happens next

blocks.text: Lead with the answer

Many reports tell the story in the order the work was done: we collected data, then cleaned it, then calculated. Readers prefer the opposite. Start with your main message in one sentence, then give two or three supporting numbers, then one chart, then your recommendation. Put the method and detailed tables at the end or in an attachment for those who want to check.

blocks.title: The one-page report structure
items: Main message first
Two or three numbers
One clear chart
What it means
What we should do
blocks.caption: This order respects the reader's time and makes the action impossible to miss.

blocks.name: presentation
blocks.alt: A woman presenting a chart to an audience
blocks.caption: Lead with the answer and support it with a few numbers and one honest chart.

blocks.text: Presenting in a meeting

items: **Open with the question and the answer** in under a minute: "We asked why deliveries were late. The main reason is group orders."
**Show one chart at a time** and say what to look at: "Look at the September bar, it is the tallest."
**Read numbers slowly and round them.** Say "about one in eight orders" rather than "11.9 percent" when speaking.
**Stop and ask for questions** before giving the recommendation, so people feel heard.
**Close with the decision you need** and who will do what by when.

blocks.text: If you present on a phone or in a group video call, prepare the chart as a single clear image beforehand. Large text and a short message title matter even more on a small screen, and many participants may join with weak connections.
Outputs and outcomes

Donors and development partners often ask for both. **Outputs** are what you delivered: 45 women trained, 6 sessions held. **Outcomes** are the changes that followed: how many women started using the skill, earned more or kept records. Outcomes are harder to measure but matter more. Measure them with a simple follow-up, such as a phone call or form one or three months later, and report how many people you were able to reach.

blocks.title: Worked example: one set of results, two messages
blocks.context: For example, a community skills programme in Ilorin trained women in bookkeeping. Of 45 enrolled, 38 completed. In a three-month follow-up by phone, the coordinator reached all 38, and 25 said they now keep weekly sales records.
steps: Completion rate: 38 ÷ 45 × 100 = about 84.4%.
Outcome rate: 25 ÷ 38 × 100 = about 65.8% of completers keep weekly records.

Donor report headline: "Two in three graduates now keep weekly sales records three months after training." She adds the numbers, a bar chart of enrolled, completed and keeping records, the main reason 7 women did not finish (clashes with market days) and a request to fund a Saturday cohort.

WhatsApp message to members: "Thank you all! 38 of us finished the course and 25 now keep weekly records. Next cohort will meet on Saturdays so market women can join. Reply YES if you want to help mentor."
blocks.result: The same data serves both audiences. The donor sees honest outputs, outcomes and a clear funding request; members see their achievement and a concrete next step.

blocks.text: Notice that the donor version includes the 7 women who did not finish and the reason why. Leaving out disappointing numbers is tempting, but funders usually notice, and the reason for dropping out is exactly what helps design a better programme.
Writing a short data message

items: **One message per update.** Do not pack five findings into one WhatsApp message.
**Use real numbers, rounded sensibly.** "About 2 in 3" or "66%" is easier to read than 65.79%.
**Compare with something.** "₦315,000 in September, up from ₦260,000 in August" means more than one number alone.
**End with an action or question.** What do you want the reader to do?
**Attach the chart as an image**, not the whole spreadsheet, unless they need to check the details.

blocks.title: Be ready for the hard question
blocks.text: Expect someone to ask "How do you know?" Keep your workbook and data dictionary ready, and be honest about limits, such as a small sample or a follow-up that did not reach everyone. Admitting limits usually increases trust.

takeaways: Different audiences need the same truth framed for what they care about.
Main message first, then numbers, one chart, meaning and action.
Outputs are what you did; outcomes are what changed.
Short messages: one point, real numbers, a comparison and an action.
